result.scope_note: The 2019 SI (International System of Units) defines seven base units: metre for length, kilogram for mass, second for time, ampere for electric current, kelvin for thermodynamic temperature, mole for amount of substance, and candela for luminous intensity. Electric current has the ampere as its base unit, not the kelvin. The kelvin is the base unit for thermodynamic temperature.

excerpts.text: The units and their physical quantities are the [second](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second "Second") for [time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time "Time"), the [metre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metre "Metre") (also spelled meter) for [length](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Length "Length") or [distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distance "Distance"), the [kilogram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilogram "Kilogram") for [mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass "Mass"), the [ampere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ampere "Ampere") for [electric current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_current "Electric current"), the [kelvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin "Kelvin") for [thermodynamic temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermodynamic_temperature "Thermodynamic temperature"), the [mole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mole_(unit) "Mole (unit)") for [amount of substance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amount_of_substance "Amount of substance"), and the [candela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candela "Candela") for [luminous intensity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luminous_intensity "Luminous intensity").

excerpts.text: The ampere (A), the SI base unit of electric current, is a familiar and indispensable quantity in everyday life.

In November 2018, however, the redefinition of the ampere ― along with three other [SI base units](https://www.nist.gov/si-redefinition/definitions-si-base-units): the kilogram (mass), kelvin (temperature) and mole (amount of substance) ― was approved. Starting on May 20, 2019, the ampere is based on a fundamental physical constant: the elementary charge (e), which is the amount of electric charge in a single electron (negative) or proton (positive).
